transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Hi, yes, thank you. Thank you for seeing me. I know I probably should have come in sooner, but, well, it's hard to explain exactly. I’m a social worker—specifically, I work in mental health and substance abuse. I have my graduate degree, I’ve been in the field for years, and I’m usually the one trying to figure out what's going on with someone else, so it feels a bit strange to be on this side of things. 

But what finally brought me in, what really pushed me to make the appointment, is that I feel like... um, I feel like the part of me that used to reach for people has just gone completely quiet. I used to be so engaged. I took so much genuine pleasure in my work, in really being present for my clients, and outside of work, too. I had a really dedicated yoga practice, I loved going to art galleries on the weekends, I was always writing and journaling... I mean, I have stacks of filled journals at home. 

But lately, I look at my yoga mat and I just feel nothing. I don't want to write. The idea of going to a gallery just feels completely empty. It’s like the volume on all the things that used to bring me joy or make me want to interact with the world has been turned all the way down. Now, I’m mostly just... I'm just moving through my obligations. I get up, I go to work, I do the paperwork, I come home, but there's no spark in it anymore. I just can't seem to find my way back to caring about those things the way I used to, which is really unsettling when your whole life and career have been built on connecting with people and being active, you know? It's just this heavy, quiet blankness every day.
How long have you been feeling this way—completely without interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

Well, it hasn't been a sudden thing, you know? It didn't just happen overnight where I woke up and the color was drained out of everything. It’s been a gradual process, but if I really sit down and trace it back, I’d say this whole change in how I’m thinking, how I’m working, and especially how I’m connecting—or not connecting—with people, it’s been going on for about eight months. 

It started right around the time my husband and I had to take my older relative into our apartment. She couldn't live alone anymore, and there were a lot of family dynamics involved, a lot of discussions, and ultimately, it just made the most sense for her to come stay with us. We had to rearrange the whole apartment, move my home office into a corner of the living room, and adjust to this entirely new routine. 

At first, I thought it was just the stress of the transition. You know, caregiver burnout is a very real thing, and I see it in my clients all the time, so I told myself, "Oh, you're just adjusting, you're just tired from the extra responsibilities." I thought the lack of interest in my yoga or the galleries was just because my mental energy was being spent on figuring out her medication schedule and making sure she was comfortable. But then the weeks turned into months, and we settled into a routine with her, and the dust kind of settled... but I didn't bounce back. The heavy, quiet blankness just stayed. So yes, it’s been about eight months now since she moved in, and that’s really when all of this started taking root.
Have you ever had a distinct period—lasting several days or more—where you felt unusually energetic, elated, or needed much less sleep than usual, even if it didn't cause problems at the time?

No, no, I haven't. I know exactly what you're asking about, being in the field—you're screening for mania or hypomania, right? Looking for that bipolar piece. But no, I've never experienced anything like that. I've never had a time where I felt, you know, on top of the world or like I could run on two hours of sleep and still reorganize the entire apartment. 

Actually, I’ve always been someone who really values my sleep. Even before all this started, back when I was still doing my yoga and going to galleries, I was very protective of my rest. I need my solid eight hours, or I just don't function well the next day, especially when I have back-to-back client sessions. The mental load of social work is just too high to try and do it sleep-deprived. 

And as for feeling elated or having all this unusual energy... no. Even on my best days, before the last eight months, I was just content, you know? Grounded. I enjoyed my life, but it wasn't this buzzing, electric kind of energy. It was a calm, steady engagement with the world. And now, of course, it's just the opposite. It's just this heavy, dragging feeling. But no, to answer your question, I’ve never swung in the other direction. No periods of high energy or decreased need for sleep. Just the steady baseline I used to have, and now... well, now this.
Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself or that life isn't worth living, or noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual?

No, no, I haven't had any thoughts like that. I know that's another important thing to screen for, the suicidal ideation, especially when someone comes in describing this kind of... well, this anhedonia, this lack of joy. I see it in my clients, of course, when the depression gets so heavy that they just can't see a way out, and they start thinking about ending things. But for me, it's not like that. I don't want to die, and I don't think life isn't worth living. It's more just... I'm frustrated that I'm not living it the way I used to, if that makes sense? I want to get back to my life, I just can't seem to find the energy or the desire to do it right now. But no thoughts of hurting myself, absolutely not. 

And as for moving or speaking more slowly... no, I don't think so. I mean, I feel sluggish internally, like everything takes more effort, but I don't think it's showing up on the outside like that. My husband hasn't mentioned anything about me moving like I'm in molasses or talking in slow motion. I'm still getting through my days, still doing my sessions with clients, and you really have to stay on your toes for those. If I were really slowing down psychomotor-wise, I think I would notice it in my work, or my colleagues would say something. It's just this internal heaviness, not a physical slowing down.

Would you say you're still able to keep up with the demands of your job and daily responsibilities reasonably well, or has it become genuinely difficult for you to function—at work or at home—because of how you've been feeling?

Well, that’s the thing, isn't it? It’s... it's really starting to show, and it’s incredibly difficult for me to admit that, especially given what I do for a living. I mean, I’m still showing up to work. I haven't taken a leave of absence or started calling in sick all the time. I get up, I get dressed, I log into my computer, I do my sessions... but the quality of my work, my actual functioning, it’s just not where it needs to be. It’s genuinely difficult now. 

I’ve always prided myself on being very organized, very on top of things. When you're managing caseloads and dealing with community resources, you have to be. But lately... well, I’ve actually missed a couple of major grant deadlines. And these aren't just minor paperwork things; these are grants that help fund some of the programs my clients rely on. I had the dates on my calendar, I knew they were coming up, but I just... I would sit there staring at the application, and the words wouldn't make sense, or I just couldn't muster the executive function to pull the data together. The deadline would come and go, and I’d just feel this dull wave of guilt, but not enough to actually fix it. 

And it’s not just the administrative side, either. My supervisor... she’s wonderful, very perceptive, which is great but also terrible when you’re trying to hide that you’re falling apart. She hasn't confronted me directly, but I’ve noticed over the last month or two that she’s quietly moved some of my more demanding, high-acuity clients to other clinicians. She’ll frame it as, "Oh, I know you've got a lot on your plate right now with your mother-in-law, let’s shift this case to Sarah," but I know what’s really happening. She sees that I’m not functioning at my usual level. She sees that I don't have the emotional bandwidth to handle the intense crisis interventions right now. 

So, yes, it has become genuinely difficult. I’m going through the motions, I’m physically present, but the actual capacity to do my job the way I’m supposed to... it’s slipping away from me, and it’s terrifying because my career has always been such a huge part of my identity. And at home, it’s the same—I’m doing the bare minimum to keep the household running, but the joy of cooking or organizing, it’s just gone. So, yes, it’s definitely impacting my ability to function.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight, or trouble sleeping or concentrating, over these past eight months?

No, not really. I know those are the classic somatic symptoms you look for with depression—the sleep disturbances, the appetite changes, the cognitive fog—but honestly, that hasn't been my experience. 

My appetite is exactly the same as it's always been. I still eat my regular meals. I haven't lost any weight, haven't gained any weight. I know some people completely lose their taste for food when they get depressed, or they go the other way and start comfort eating, you know, carbs and sugar, but I just eat what I usually eat. The food doesn't necessarily bring me the same pleasure it used to—like, I used to really enjoy trying a new recipe or going out for a nice dinner with my husband, and now it's just fuel, just something I have to do to keep going—but the actual appetite is still there. 

And sleep... well, like I mentioned earlier, I've always been very protective of my sleep. I'm still getting my eight hours. I go to bed at the same time, wake up at the same time. I don't have trouble falling asleep, and I'm not waking up at three in the morning staring at the ceiling, which I know is a hallmark of melancholic depression. I'm just sleeping my normal amount. 

As for concentrating... I mean, I told you about missing those grant deadlines, but that wasn't really a concentration issue. It wasn't that I couldn't focus on the words or that I was getting easily distracted by other things. It was more just a complete lack of motivation, a lack of executive function to initiate the task and see it through. When I am actually sitting with a client, I can focus on what they're saying. I can follow their train of thought, I can track their progress, I can formulate my clinical responses. The concentration is there when I force it to be. It's just the drive, the energy behind it that's completely depleted. So, no, I wouldn't say I've had any significant changes in appetite, weight, sleep, or pure concentration. It's really just the anhedonia and the lack of energy.
Have you been experiencing feelings of worthlessness, excessive guilt, or hopelessness about your situation, and if so, how intense or pervasive have these feelings been?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I know I just said a few minutes ago that I felt a wave of guilt about missing those grant deadlines, but I want to be really clear about what that looks like for me. It was very specific, situational guilt. It was just, "Oh, I dropped the ball on this specific administrative task," not... not that pervasive, globalizing guilt where you think, "I am a terrible, worthless person who ruins everything." I definitely don't have that. When I do intakes with clients who are experiencing that kind of excessive, toxic guilt, you know, they're apologizing for things that aren't even remotely their fault, or they feel like this massive burden to their families. I don't feel like a burden at all. My husband and I are a team, and I know I still contribute, even if I'm just doing the bare minimum around the house right now. 

And as for worthlessness... absolutely not. I know I have value. I have my master's, I have years and years of experience in the trenches of social work, I know I'm a highly competent clinician. Even with my supervisor quietly shifting my high-acuity caseload, I don't sit there thinking I'm useless or incompetent. My core sense of self-esteem is actually completely intact, which in a way makes this whole experience even more frustrating! I know exactly how capable I am, I just... I can't seem to execute it right now. The engine is just stalled, but I know the car itself isn't broken, if that makes sense. 

And hopelessness... no, I'm not hopeless. I mean, I'm sitting right here talking to you, aren't I? If I were truly hopeless about my situation, I wouldn't have bothered making this appointment or trying to figure out what's going on with my brain. I still fundamentally believe things can get better. I preach it to my clients every single day—that things shift, that people heal—and I do apply that to myself. I don't feel like
Have you noticed a persistent lack of energy or feeling fatigued throughout the day, even when you haven't been physically exerting yourself?

You know, I’ve actually spent a lot of time analyzing this exact distinction in my own head recently, because as a clinician, you're always trying to parse out exactly what a symptom really means in practice. And the short answer is no, I really don't have that persistent lack of energy or that physical fatigue. It’s not that heavy, leaden feeling in my limbs, you know? I still have the exact same physical stamina I’ve always had. 

I mean, I’m forty-nine, so I’m not exactly running marathons on the weekends or anything, but I can easily get through my day without needing a nap or feeling physically drained. I get up, I take my shower, I walk from the parking garage all the way across the clinic campus, I can sit through back-to-back sessions without feeling like my body is going to give out on me. 

It's really important to me to differentiate between physical fatigue and what I was describing earlier as that lack of drive or motivation. Because the energy is absolutely there. The battery is fully charged, so to speak. If there were a sudden emergency—like if one of my clients escalated in the waiting room and I needed to physically jump up and run down the hall to intervene or grab security—I could do it without a second thought. My body isn't tired at all. 

It's just that, under normal, everyday circumstances, when I'm just looking at a stack of grant applications or thinking about making dinner for my husband, the actual desire to expend that energy is completely absent. It's an apathy thing, not an energy thing. But the physical energy itself? No, that's completely intact. I don't feel fatigued or physically sluggish at all during the day.
Aside from the loss of interest and drive you've described, have you noticed feeling sad, down, or empty inside on most days, even if you can't always point to why?

No, and that is a really important distinction that I’ve been analyzing in my own head, because people always just assume that if you've lost your drive, you must be sitting around crying all day. But I don't feel sad at all. I really don't. I don't have that heavy, tearful, down-in-the-dumps feeling. My husband, bless his heart, he keeps asking me, "Honey, are you sad? Did something happen at the clinic?" And I have to keep trying to explain to him that it's just not an emotional thing like that. I'm not walking around feeling miserable or sorry for myself. 

And as for feeling empty... you know, emptiness is such a specific, heavy word. When some of the clients I work with talk about emptiness, they usually mean this painful, hollow void in their chest that they desperately need to fill, and it causes them so much active distress. I don't have that whatsoever. I don't feel hollow or empty inside. I feel completely normal emotionally. If I see something on the news that's tragic, I feel an appropriate, normal amount of sadness about it, but my baseline everyday mood isn't sad. 

It's really fascinating, honestly, from a professional standpoint, to experience this complete separation of your motivation and your actual mood. Because you always assume they go hand-in-hand, right? You assume if someone isn't keeping up with their paperwork or engaging in their usual weekend stuff, they must be feeling just profoundly low. But I'm not low. I'm really not. I'm just sort of... existing without that forward momentum I usually have. So no, I wouldn't say I feel sad or empty on most days at all. It's purely that lack of drive we were just talking about.
